power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Machines in the Middle: How AI Use Changes What Coworkers Think of, and Do for, One Another

text.text: Generative AI is now embedded in how coworkers, leaders, and organizations communicate, yet its effects on the relationships among them are still poorly understood.

This review synthesizes recent research on how an individual's AI use changes the way others perceive, judge, and behave toward them, and shows that these effects can be explained by established theories of human-human interaction, including attribution theory, computers-as-social-actors, the integrative model of organizational trust, social exchange theory, and resourcebased theories.

The evidence suggests that observers often read AI use as a sign of disposition rather than circumstance, judging AI users as less competent, motivated, warm, and authentic, and that disclosure does not repair the resulting loss of trust.

These perceptions carry over into behavior: coworkers reciprocate less, share less knowledge, and show less prosocial behavior toward AI users, while AI-related job insecurity, loneliness, and work alienation further strain ties among colleagues.
AI use also loosens moral standards and shifts how blame is assigned, making people more critical of others' work but more lenient toward misconduct.
These effects are conditional rather than uniformly negative.

AI can reduce loneliness, improve coordination, and prompt employees to invest more in emotionally supportive ties, and relational buffers such as leader-member exchange, shared leadership, and supervisor support can offset its costs.
The review concludes that AI's costs to workplace relationships run mainly through indirect pathways, not through the technology itself.

It outlines organizational implications, including clear norms for when and why AI is used and protection of socially valued tasks, and identifies priorities for future research: longitudinal designs, team-and network-level studies, intervention research, and more diverse samples.

As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes integrated into the workplace, from drafting emails and offering advice to managing performance, its impact extends beyond task assistance to the relationships people form with one another.

AI is now positioned between coworkers, between leaders and followers, and between employees and their organizations, mediating the exchanges that have traditionally defined workplace relationships (Boyd & Markowitz, 2026; Jung et al., 2026).
text.formatted: AI is now positioned between coworkers, between leaders and followers, and between employees and their organizations, mediating the exchanges that have traditionally defined workplace relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Boyd & Markowitz, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Jung et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The central claim of this review is that an individual's AI use indirectly changes how other people perceive, judge, and behave toward them in systematic and predictable ways, and these changes can be understood through existing psychological theories of human-human interaction.
People who do not use AI trust AI users less and see AI users as less competent, less motivated, and less authentic (Cardon & Coman, 2025; Reif et al., 2025; Schilke & Reimann, 2025).
text.formatted: People who do not use AI trust AI users less and see AI users as less competent, less motivated, and less authentic <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Cardon & Coman, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Reif et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Schilke & Reimann, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: People judge AI users more harshly: AI-assisted effort is read as less warm, less empathetic, and less personally motivated, and interacting with AI can itself make people harsher judges of others (Buss et al., 2025; Dishop et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023; Tey et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026b).

text.text: Additionally, people change how they behave toward AI users, reciprocating help less, sharing less knowledge, and being less prosocial toward those who rely on AI (Dang & Liu, 2026b; Dishop et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Additionally, people change how they behave toward AI users, reciprocating help less, sharing less knowledge, and being less prosocial toward those who rely on AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dang & Liu, 2026b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Dishop et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Xu et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Zhou et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Over time, such shifts may weaken people's motivation to invest in relationships with colleagues, make interactions more transactional, erode relational skills and tacit knowledge, and contribute to incivility and reduced wellbeing at work (Cebulla, 2025; Connell, 2025; Keeler & Murphy, 2026).

text.text: However, AI use in the workplace is not uniformly negative.
Under some conditions, AI use can lead to more favorable performance evaluations (He et al., 2024).

text.text: Additionally, when AI reduces the need for task-based exchange, employees may compensate by investing more in emotionally supportive ties with coworkers (Zhang & Yan, 2026) and by helping coworkers more to meet a heightened need for affiliation (Tang et al., 2023).

text.text: The social presence of AI can reduce workplace loneliness under some conditions (Liu et al., 2025); AI-generated support messages can be rated as more sincere and actionable than human ones (Swain et al., 2025), and can improve coordination among human groups (Shirado & Christakis, 2017).
text.formatted: The social presence of AI can reduce workplace loneliness under some conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Liu et al., 2025)</ref>; AI-generated support messages can be rated as more sincere and actionable than human ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Swain et al., 2025)</ref>, and can improve coordination among human groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Shirado & Christakis, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, the literature suggests that AI's relational effects are conditional.
AI can support coordination and reduce routine work, but it also changes how employees interpret one another's effort, care, competence, and responsibility.
People interpret others' behavior in systematic, predictable ways, and much of AI's effect on workplace relationships can be understood within existing psychological theory.

Attribution theory offers the most useful starting point, because the primary question an observer asks when a coworker uses AI is why they used it, and what that says about them (Reif et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; He et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2026; Jago et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Attribution theory offers the most useful starting point, because the primary question an observer asks when a coworker uses AI is why they used it, and what that says about them <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Reif et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Zhou et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">He et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Hu et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Jago et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Two well-established attribution biases help explain why AI use so often counts against the user in the eyes of others, and why people tend to see their own AI use as reasonable while viewing others' use of the same tools as a problem.
The first is the fundamental attribution error, the tendency to overemphasize internal traits and underweight situational factors when explaining other people's behavior (Ross, 1977).
text.formatted: The first is the fundamental attribution error, the tendency to overemphasize internal traits and underweight situational factors when explaining other people's behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Ross, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: Applied to AI, an observer who sees a coworker use AI is likely to read it as a sign of disposition, such as laziness, low competence, or low commitment, rather than as a response to workload, deadlines, or organizational expectations.

This is consistent with evidence that AI users are rated as less competent and less motivated than non-users (Reif et al., 2025), that people deny humanness to those who seek advice from AI (Dang & Liu, 2026b), and that observers assign responsibility for both success and failure in human-AI collaboration to the person rather than the AI (Hu et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This is consistent with evidence that AI users are rated as less competent and less motivated than non-users <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Reif et al., 2025)</ref>, that people deny humanness to those who seek advice from AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dang & Liu, 2026b)</ref>, and that observers assign responsibility for both success and failure in human-AI collaboration to the person rather than the AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hu et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The second is the self-serving bias, the tendency to attribute one's own successes to internal qualities such as skill and effort and one's failures to external circumstances (Miller & Ross, 1975).
text.formatted: The second is the self-serving bias, the tendency to attribute one's own successes to internal qualities such as skill and effort and one's failures to external circumstances <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Miller & Ross, 1975)</ref>.

text.text: For AI users, this bias allows good AI-assisted outcomes to be claimed as one's own work while poor outcomes can be blamed on the tool.
For observers, the same logic runs in reverse: a coworker's AI-assisted success is discounted as the AI's contribution while their failures remain their own.
Together, these biases suggest that the same act of AI use carries very different meaning depending on whether one is the user or the observer.
Several other frameworks recur across this literature and are drawn on where relevant in the sections that follow.

Understanding how people interact and relate to computers through the paradigm computers are social actors is akin to how people interact with each other; when people are interacting with AI, all the same social scripts and heuristics are triggered that would normally happen in a human-human interaction despite the lack of human connection.

In other words, humans' interpersonal social rules, norms, and expectations are ingrained in how they behave, which comes naturally and automatically without the need to actually view computers (or AI) as human (Nass et al., 1994).
text.formatted: In other words, humans' interpersonal social rules, norms, and expectations are ingrained in how they behave, which comes naturally and automatically without the need to actually view computers (or AI) as human <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Nass et al., 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, it can be expected that AI interactions can help inform later human-human interactions.

The integrative model of organizational trust (Mayer et al., 1995) separates trustworthiness into ability, benevolence, and integrity, and has been used to explain why AI use erodes per-ceptions of a user's benevolence and integrity even when their ability is unaffected (Dang & Liu, 2026a; Cardon & Coman, 2025; Schilke & Reimann, 2025).
text.formatted: The integrative model of organizational trust <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Mayer et al., 1995)</ref> separates trustworthiness into ability, benevolence, and integrity, and has been used to explain why AI use erodes per-ceptions of a user's benevolence and integrity even when their ability is unaffected <ref type="bibr">(Dang & Liu, 2026a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Cardon & Coman, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Schilke & Reimann, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The social exchange theory as a cost-benefit analysis of human interaction explains why AI-assisted help is reciprocated less than unassisted help because people may perceive people who use AI as dampening the ''cost'' of the help (Dishop et al., 2025; Zhang & Yan, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b; Harrell & Traeger, 2025a). Dang and Liu's (2026a) model of AI-use-induced dehumanization and resource-based theories, including the conservation of resources theory and the job demands-resources model, explain loneliness, alienation, and conflict as products of AI-driven resource depletion (Tang et al., 2023; Hai et al., 2025; Jeong & Jeong, 2025; Liu et al., 2026).

text.text: Across all of these frameworks, AI's relational effects are rarely direct; they are filtered through attribution, trust, exchange, and resource processes that were well understood in human-human contexts before AI entered the picture.
One of the most direct ways AI changes workplace relationships is by reducing the need to interact with coworkers.

When AI can easily carry out tasks that once required a colleague's help, the everyday exchanges that build and maintain coworker relationships become less necessary (Dishop et al., 2025; Zhang & Yan, 2026).
text.formatted: When AI can easily carry out tasks that once required a colleague's help, the everyday exchanges that build and maintain coworker relationships become less necessary <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dishop et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Zhang & Yan, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Whether this matters for employees' sense of connection depends on whether AI can adequately stand in for the human contact it replaces, and the evidence on this point is mixed.
In some cases, AI is an adequate substitute for human interaction.

For example, Ho et al. (2018) find that the emotional and relational benefits of self-disclosure are equivalent whether people believe they are disclosing to a chatbot or to another person, supporting the computers are social actors paradigm (Nass et al., 1994). Liu et al. (2025) find that the social presence of AI reduces employee workplace loneliness through AI rapport and interpersonal closeness, although this effect depends on the employee's underlying need for human interaction. Swain et al. (2025) tested an LLM-based ''empathetic coworker'' designed to help client-service representatives regulate emotion after uncivil client interactions; representatives rated its support as more sincere and actionable than human-generated messages.

text.text: Yet, the same representatives emphasized the indispensability of shared experience, suggesting that AI can supplement but not fully replace a coworker.
The limits of substitution are also clear in initial interactions, where people are less open, agreeable, and self-disclosing with AI than with humans (Mou & Xu, 2017).
text.formatted: The limits of substitution are also clear in initial interactions, where people are less open, agreeable, and self-disclosing with AI than with humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Mou & Xu, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, AI-generated messages made recipients feel more heard than human-generated ones, but only when recipients believed the message came from a person; once they learned it came from AI, the feeling of being heard diminished (Yin et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Similarly, AI-generated messages made recipients feel more heard than human-generated ones, but only when recipients believed the message came from a person; once they learned it came from AI, the feeling of being heard diminished <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Yin et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Feeling heard therefore appears to be a relational function that cannot be replaced by AI even when AI performs the task equally well or better.
In other cases, AI contributes to loneliness and alienation.

As employees interact more with AI in pursuit of work goals, they experience both a compensatory need for social affiliation and a sense of loneliness, which worsens after-work insomnia and alcohol consumption especially among employees high in attachment anxiety (Tang et al., 2023).
text.formatted: As employees interact more with AI in pursuit of work goals, they experience both a compensatory need for social affiliation and a sense of loneliness, which worsens after-work insomnia and alcohol consumption especially among employees high in attachment anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Tang et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: AI can threaten the psychological need for relatedness at work, alongside the needs for competence and autonomy, prompting employees to adopt maladaptive coping strategies (Hermann et al., 2025).
text.formatted: AI can threaten the psychological need for relatedness at work, alongside the needs for competence and autonomy, prompting employees to adopt maladaptive coping strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hermann et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Daily employee-AI collaboration also increases work alienation, a disconnection from work and colleagues when digital job demands are high (Hai et al., 2025), and AI use more broadly is linked to psychological distress through the dual paths of job insecurity and workplace loneliness (Liu et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Daily employee-AI collaboration also increases work alienation, a disconnection from work and colleagues when digital job demands are high <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hai et al., 2025)</ref>, and AI use more broadly is linked to psychological distress through the dual paths of job insecurity and workplace loneliness <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Liu et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These effects are not evenly distributed; AI use is associated with more loneliness overall, but the effect is stronger for older adults than for younger ones (Dong et al., 2025).
text.formatted: These effects are not evenly distributed; AI use is associated with more loneliness overall, but the effect is stronger for older adults than for younger ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dong et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Although loneliness and alienation are measured as individual-level traits, they reflect how connected people feel to those around them, so rising loneliness alongside greater AI use may signal that workplace relationships are under strain.
However, relationships depend not only on how employees feel when they use AI but also on how others interpret that use, and AI use changes those perceptions as well.

Trust and perceived authenticity are foundations of a cooperative and productive workplace (De Jong et al., 2016; Mayer et al., 1995; McAllister, 1995); employees need to trust their coworkers and leaders to be confident in shared decisions, but AI use appears to weaken both aspects.
text.formatted: Trust and perceived authenticity are foundations of a cooperative and productive workplace <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(De Jong et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Mayer et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">McAllister, 1995)</ref>; employees need to trust their coworkers and leaders to be confident in shared decisions, but AI use appears to weaken both aspects.

text.text: When people doubt the authenticity of others' communication, they also report feeling a loss of agency in the exchange, which can undermine communication between coworkers (Connell, 2025; Wenker, 2023).
text.formatted: When people doubt the authenticity of others' communication, they also report feeling a loss of agency in the exchange, which can undermine communication between coworkers <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Connell, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Wenker, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: People tend to distrust others who use AI and perceive them as less warm, even when AI users explicitly disclose their use (Schilke & Reimann, 2025; Yin et al., 2024).
text.formatted: People tend to distrust others who use AI and perceive them as less warm, even when AI users explicitly disclose their use <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Schilke & Reimann, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Yin et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: People also question others' authorship, confidence, and sincerity when they know AI was involved (Buss et al., 2025; Cardon & Coman, 2025).
text.formatted: People also question others' authorship, confidence, and sincerity when they know AI was involved <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Buss et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Cardon & Coman, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with the integrative model of organizational trust (Mayer et al., 1995), this affects perceived benevolence and integrity rather than ability; AI users as a class are judged as less benevolent than non-users regardless of their actual competence (Dang & Liu, 2026a).
text.formatted: Consistent with the integrative model of organizational trust <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Mayer et al., 1995)</ref>, this affects perceived benevolence and integrity rather than ability; AI users as a class are judged as less benevolent than non-users regardless of their actual competence <ref type="bibr">(Dang & Liu, 2026a)</ref>.

text.text: Even outside of the workplace, using AI advice for relational maintenance in friendships is perceived as low effort and is related to lower relationship satisfaction and higher uncertainty (Liu et al., 2023), which translate into harsher judgments.
text.formatted: Even outside of the workplace, using AI advice for relational maintenance in friendships is perceived as low effort and is related to lower relationship satisfaction and higher uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Liu et al., 2023)</ref>, which translate into harsher judgments.

text.text: People who use AI at work both anticipate and actually receive lower ratings of competence and motivation, and they are seen as lazier than those who refrain, with downstream consequences for hiring evaluations (Reif et al., 2025).
text.formatted: People who use AI at work both anticipate and actually receive lower ratings of competence and motivation, and they are seen as lazier than those who refrain, with downstream consequences for hiring evaluations <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Reif et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, people who have just completed a task with an AI subsequently judge an unrelated human's work more harshly than people who worked with a purported human partner, suggesting that interacting with AI recalibrates the standards people apply to others (Tey et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Furthermore, people who have just completed a task with an AI subsequently judge an unrelated human's work more harshly than people who worked with a purported human partner, suggesting that interacting with AI recalibrates the standards people apply to others <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Tey et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: How AI affects relationships is predicated on both the task type and the relationship context.
People prefer AI when it is used for functionally relevant tasks and prefer humans when a task is socially or empathically relevant (Höddinghaus et al., 2021; Li & Bitterly, 2024; Lindgren, 2024).
text.formatted: People prefer AI when it is used for functionally relevant tasks and prefer humans when a task is socially or empathically relevant <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Höddinghaus et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Li & Bitterly, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Lindgren, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, employees who have strong relationships with their coworkers interpret those coworkers' AI use as a challenge, whereas those with weak relationships interpret it as a threat and orient toward avoiding negative job outcomes rather than pursuing positive ones (Qu & Xu, 2026).
text.formatted: Additionally, employees who have strong relationships with their coworkers interpret those coworkers' AI use as a challenge, whereas those with weak relationships interpret it as a threat and orient toward avoiding negative job outcomes rather than pursuing positive ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Qu & Xu, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, relationships can change how people interpret AI use, which is seen in supervisor relationships as well.

Supervisors inflate performance ratings for employees who use AI, attributing AI-assisted output to the employee's own skill (He et al., 2024), yet being managed by an algorithm, rather than assisted by one, lowers the perceived status of the managed employee because it signals that the underlying job lacks complexity (Jago et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Supervisors inflate performance ratings for employees who use AI, attributing AI-assisted output to the employee's own skill <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(He et al., 2024</ref>), yet being managed by an algorithm, rather than assisted by one, lowers the perceived status of the managed employee because it signals that the underlying job lacks complexity <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Jago et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, people assign this credit and blame asymmetrically, attributing both success and failure in human-AI collaboration to the person rather than to the AI (Hu et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Furthermore, people assign this credit and blame asymmetrically, attributing both success and failure in human-AI collaboration to the person rather than to the AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hu et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, disclosure, the remedy most often proposed to offset these costs, does not restore trust.
Disclosing AI use lowers trust in the discloser regardless of how the disclosure is framed or whether it is voluntary (Schilke & Reimann, 2025).
text.formatted: Disclosing AI use lowers trust in the discloser regardless of how the disclosure is framed or whether it is voluntary <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Schilke & Reimann, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: AI use therefore does not carry a single, fixed social meaning at work; its effect on how a person is trusted, judged, and credited depends on the task, the relationship between observer and user, and whether AI is understood as replacing the person's judgment, augmenting their effort, or managing them.
AI use also shifts moral standards more broadly.
People tend to apply different moral beliefs to robots compared to the moral beliefs they apply to humans (Malle et al., 2015).
text.formatted: People tend to apply different moral beliefs to robots compared to the moral beliefs they apply to humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Malle et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Employees' AI usage triggers more flexible moral beliefs, which increases their own workplace deviance and produces more lenient moral judgment of other people's misconduct (Zhao et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Employees' AI usage triggers more flexible moral beliefs, which increases their own workplace deviance and produces more lenient moral judgment of other people's misconduct <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Zhao et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Akin to human interactions, AI-generated advice that promotes dishonesty increases dishonest behavior in the person who receives it (Leib et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Akin to human interactions, AI-generated advice that promotes dishonesty increases dishonest behavior in the person who receives it <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Leib et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Employees who self-identify as AI users report higher psychological entitlement, which increases unethical behavior toward others; this effect is strongest when AI identity is perceived as rare within the organization, suggesting that being an early or unusual adopter amplifies the sense of being special (Cao et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Employees who self-identify as AI users report higher psychological entitlement, which increases unethical behavior toward others; this effect is strongest when AI identity is perceived as rare within the organization, suggesting that being an early or unusual adopter amplifies the sense of being special <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Cao et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, AI can loosen the moral standards people hold, both for themselves and for others, which may make unethical behavior easier to cognitively justify, thus increasing moral flexibility at work.

When people turn to AI to make sense of social and moral situations, AI generated responses can change the conclusions they would otherwise have reached on their own or through conversation with another person.

Large language models (LLMs) tend to resolve ambiguous interpersonal situations, such as unclear signals from a supervisor or an ambiguous exchange with a colleague, into a single, confident narrative rather than preserving the uncertainty that may be warranted (Yuan et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Large language models (LLMs) tend to resolve ambiguous interpersonal situations, such as unclear signals from a supervisor or an ambiguous exchange with a colleague, into a single, confident narrative rather than preserving the uncertainty that may be warranted <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Yuan et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The result is a more black-and-white view of the situation, delivered with more confidence than the evidence supports, so people may act on a false sense of interpersonal clarity.

Where a conversation with a coworker might surface alternative interpretations or situational explanations, an AI's single answer can shortcut that process, which may reinforce the tendency to attribute others' behavior to fixed traits.
Beyond loosening the moral standards people apply to themselves, AI can also alter the standards they hold others to.

People are less likely to blame AI for unfair treatment compared to blaming humans for the same treatment, and this effect has consequences for subsequent behavior; people are less likely to punish humans for unfair behavior, even when that behavior is unrelated to AI (Zhang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: People are less likely to blame AI for unfair treatment compared to blaming humans for the same treatment, and this effect has consequences for subsequent behavior; people are less likely to punish humans for unfair behavior, even when that behavior is unrelated to AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Zhang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Moral perception is therefore not only shaped by what AI says but by who people believe is responsible; when AI is involved, blame is redistributed in ways that can lower the standards people hold others to.
Whether these shifts make people more lenient or more harsh depends on the domain.
For example, AI exposure can make people more demanding judges of others' work quality (Tey et al., 2024) while making them more lenient toward others' ethical misconduct (Zhao et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For example, AI exposure can make people more demanding judges of others' work quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Tey et al., 2024)</ref> while making them more lenient toward others' ethical misconduct <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Zhao et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This may be especially harmful for workplace relationships, as colleagues could become more critical of each other's work but less willing to hold each other accountable for unfair or unethical behavior.
Toward Others?
Because attitudes are predictive of behavior, changes in how people perceive and judge AI users matter since they shape how people behave toward others.
People are less likely to show prosocial responses to those who seek advice from AI than to those who do not (Dang & Liu, 2026b).
text.formatted: People are less likely to show prosocial responses to those who seek advice from AI than to those who do not <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dang & Liu, 2026b)</ref>.

text.text: From a social exchange perspective, when AI replaces or mediates human interaction, it lowers the effort those interactions require, which may lead people to value them less and reciprocate less (Dishop et al., 2025).
text.formatted: From a social exchange perspective, when AI replaces or mediates human interaction, it lowers the effort those interactions require, which may lead people to value them less and reciprocate less <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dishop et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: When employees use AI to help coworkers, recipients perceive the helper as exerting less effort and having less benevolent intentions, which reduces the gratitude recipients feel and makes them less likely to reciprocate (Zhang et al., 2026b).
text.formatted: When employees use AI to help coworkers, recipients perceive the helper as exerting less effort and having less benevolent intentions, which reduces the gratitude recipients feel and makes them less likely to reciprocate <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Zhang et al., 2026b)</ref>.

text.text: AI-assisted help can thus weaken coworker relationships even when AI is useful, because it is read as more instrumental and less personally motivated. Harrell and Traeger (2025a, 2025b) extend this to networks of reciprocity and cooperation: adding bots to a reputationbased reciprocity network makes people less generous overall, in part because people do not believe bots deserve help the way humans do and extend that belief to humans who help bots.
text.formatted: AI-assisted help can thus weaken coworker relationships even when AI is useful, because it is read as more instrumental and less personally motivated. <ref type="bibr">Harrell and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Traeger (2025a, 2025b)</ref> extend this to networks of reciprocity and cooperation: adding bots to a reputationbased reciprocity network makes people less generous overall, in part because people do not believe bots deserve help the way humans do and extend that belief to humans who help bots.

text.text: Delegating tasks to AI may therefore dilute the social connections that are essential to workplace functioning and collaboration.
Knowledge sharing follows a similar pattern, showing that higher AI usage is related to less knowledge sharing with coworkers (Xu et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Knowledge sharing follows a similar pattern, showing that higher AI usage is related to less knowledge sharing with coworkers <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Xu et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This effect may be mediated by self-esteem.
For example, an employee's perception of a coworker's AI usage lowers their own organization-based self-esteem and raises anxiety, which increases knowledge hiding toward others (Xu et al., 2026).
text.formatted: For example, an employee's perception of a coworker's AI usage lowers their own organization-based self-esteem and raises anxiety, which increases knowledge hiding toward others <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Xu et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: AI usage at work is also associated with more time theft and job insecurity, and AIinduced job insecurity reduces the psychological safety needed for open knowledge sharing (Xu et al., 2025a; Kim & Kim, 2024).
text.formatted: AI usage at work is also associated with more time theft and job insecurity, and AIinduced job insecurity reduces the psychological safety needed for open knowledge sharing <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Xu et al., 2025a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Kim & Kim, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Frequent AI interaction is further linked to workplace incivility through job insecurity and work alienation (Yam et al., 2022; You et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Frequent AI interaction is further linked to workplace incivility through job insecurity and work alienation <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Yam et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">You et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: At the organizational level, AI investment itself, independent of any single employee's AI use, is associated with job insecurity across the workforce, which increases both coworker conflict and work-family conflict (Jeong & Jeong, 2025).
text.formatted: At the organizational level, AI investment itself, independent of any single employee's AI use, is associated with job insecurity across the workforce, which increases both coworker conflict and work-family conflict <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Jeong & Jeong, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that AI often harms coworker relationships not through the technology itself, but by threatening employees' sense of security and worth, which leads them to guard their knowledge, withdraw from colleagues, and treat one another less civilly.

These behavioral effects are not uniformly negative, and several conditions determine their direction. Zhang and Yan (2026) find that AI usage reduces instrumental ties, coworker relationships centered on task support and information access, which in turn reduces help seeking and reciprocity; but AI usage is also associated with stronger expressive ties, relationships centered on emotional support and belonging, which are linked to more help seeking and reciprocity.
text.formatted: These behavioral effects are not uniformly negative, and several conditions determine their direction. <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Zhang and Yan (2026)</ref> find that AI usage reduces instrumental ties, coworker relationships centered on task support and information access, which in turn reduces help seeking and reciprocity; but AI usage is also associated with stronger expressive ties, relationships centered on emotional support and belonging, which are linked to more help seeking and reciprocity.

text.text: Shared leadership among colleagues weakens AI's negative effect on both kinds of ties.

Employees may therefore compensate for fewer task-based interactions by investing more in emotional connection, just as the heightened affiliation need that follows AI interaction can increase helping toward coworkers (Tang et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Employees may therefore compensate for fewer task-based interactions by investing more in emotional connection, just as the heightened affiliation need that follows AI interaction can increase helping toward coworkers <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Tang et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Positive AI interactions can also carry positive spillover: expressing gratitude directed at a robot promotes prosocial behavior toward people (Xu et al., 2025b), and wellplaced bots can improve coordination among human groups (Shirado & Christakis, 2017).
text.formatted: Positive AI interactions can also carry positive spillover: expressing gratitude directed at a robot promotes prosocial behavior toward people <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Xu et al., 2025b)</ref>, and wellplaced bots can improve coordination among human groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Shirado & Christakis, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: AI does not simply reduce the total volume of coworker exchange; it reallocates which kinds of exchange happen, toward some relationships and away from others.

The perception, judgment, and behavior effects described above take on additional features in teams and leadership relationships, where AI affects not only dyads but group processes and the distribution of influence.

In three-person teams using virtual reality, the role assigned to an AI system (i.e., advisor/unsolicited advice vs. assistant/solicited advice) and its voice (i.e., male vs. female) affected who submitted the team's decisions.

When the AI was assigned an advisor role, it shaped how team members related to one another, with the advisor's voice shifting which gender took charge of submitting decisions, even though teams followed its suggestions less (Traeger et al., 2026).
text.formatted: When the AI was assigned an advisor role, it shaped how team members related to one another, with the advisor's voice shifting which gender took charge of submitting decisions, even though teams followed its suggestions less <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Traeger et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that AI does not need to be trusted or followed to affect workplace relationships.

Much of this effect is driven by belief rather than by AI's actual behavior; in teams ostensibly composed entirely of humans, simply believing that a teammate was an AI changed team sentiment, team process, and the emergence of shared cognition among the human members (Musick et al., 2021).

text.text: This mirrors the dyadic findings on disclosure and source beliefs (Yin et al., 2024; Schilke & Reimann, 2025), what people think AI is doing matters as much, if not more, than what it actually does.

text.text: When leaders adopt the use of AI, it contributes to whether employees feel threatened or supported.

Transformational leadership increases employee AI usage through perceived organizational support, though this indirect effect is weaker in highly competitive workplace environments (Wang et al., 2025). Nanda (2026) introduces the construct of algorithmic deference, the tendency to defer to algorithmic recommendations, and finds that it lowers psychological safety and innovation; positive leader-member exchange buffers this effect, suggesting that a strong leader-follower relationship can protect against some of AI's negative effects.

text.text: Shared leadership among colleagues similarly weakens AI's negative effect on coworker ties (Zhang & Yan, 2026).
text.formatted: Shared leadership among colleagues similarly weakens AI's negative effect on coworker ties <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Zhang & Yan, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Supervisor and colleague support can also determine whether AI-delivered feedback is effective; negative feedback from AI improved employees' occupational self-efficacy only when they also perceived high emotional support from supervisors and colleagues, whereas positive feedback from AI improved self-efficacy regardless of how much support employees perceived (Watanabe et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Supervisor and colleague support can also determine whether AI-delivered feedback is effective; negative feedback from AI improved employees' occupational self-efficacy only when they also perceived high emotional support from supervisors and colleagues, whereas positive feedback from AI improved self-efficacy regardless of how much support employees perceived <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Watanabe et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, the human relationships surrounding an AI tool may matter more than the tool's design in determining its effects.

AI also creates new sources of conflict and changes what is needed from leaders. Gonzalez et al. (2024) argue that as AI takes over routine communication and reporting, people who lead organizational change will rely more on distinctly human skills, such as building strong relationships and creating meaningful in-person connection, which they call communal co-presence.
text.formatted: AI also creates new sources of conflict and changes what is needed from leaders. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Gonzalez et al. (2024)</ref> argue that as AI takes over routine communication and reporting, people who lead organizational change will rely more on distinctly human skills, such as building strong relationships and creating meaningful in-person connection, which they call communal co-presence.

text.text: Similarly, Shanmugam et al. (2026) argue that AI-related conflict, such as conflict caused by algorithmic bias, surveillance, or unclear AI decisions, cannot be managed through technical fixes alone, and that HR policy, ethical oversight, and employee training all shape whether these conflicts escalate or are resolved.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Shanmugam et al. (2026)</ref> argue that AI-related conflict, such as conflict caused by algorithmic bias, surveillance, or unclear AI decisions, cannot be managed through technical fixes alone, and that HR policy, ethical oversight, and employee training all shape whether these conflicts escalate or are resolved.

text.text: Together, these perspectives suggest that as AI takes on more tasks, the human side of leadership becomes more important.
These findings carry direct implications for how organizations approach AI adoption.

Because AI's relational costs run through attribution, trust, and reciprocity rather than through output quality, organizations cannot treat AI adoption as a purely technical or productivity decision.

AI's relational risks, including lower trust between colleagues, reduced reciprocity and knowledge sharing, greater loneliness and alienation, less civil treatment of one another, and a weaker willingness to hold one another accountable, should be treated as a work health and safety concern rather than left to informal norms, and addressed through participatory job crafting that positions workers as co-designers of AI-related change rather than passive recipients of it (Cebulla, 2025).

text.text: Industrial-organizational and consulting psychology practitioners have a parallel ethical duty to anticipate and mitigate AI's interpersonal and well-being harms, not only to deliver its productivity benefits (Connell, 2025).
text.formatted: Industrial-organizational and consulting psychology practitioners have a parallel ethical duty to anticipate and mitigate AI's interpersonal and well-being harms, not only to deliver its productivity benefits <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Connell, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: People may judge AI users harshly partly because they cannot see why the AI was used.
Without that context, observers tend to assume the person is lazy or less capable, rather than considering reasons such as heavy workloads or tasks that AI is well suited for.
Supporting this, the judgment given for using AI disappears when AI is described as clearly useful for the task (Reif et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Supporting this, the judgment given for using AI disappears when AI is described as clearly useful for the task <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Reif et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Organizations could therefore reduce this judgment by setting clear, shared norms about when and why AI use is expected, so that AI use is seen as part of the job rather than a personal shortcoming.
This may matter more than disclosure, since simply revealing AI use does not restore trust (Schilke & Reimann, 2025).
text.formatted: This may matter more than disclosure, since simply revealing AI use does not restore trust <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Schilke & Reimann, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Since disclosure alone does not restore trust (Schilke & Reimann, 2025), relational remedies might be more promising: investing in leader-member exchange (Nanda, 2026), shared leadership (Zhang & Yan, 2026), supportive supervisors and colleagues (Watanabe et al., 2025), and HRM practices could reduce AI-driven job insecurity (Jeong & Jeong, 2025).

text.text: Organizations should also consider protecting the tasks where human contact is most valued, such as socially and empathically relevant exchanges (Li & Bitterly, 2024), rather than automating them by default.
text.formatted: Organizations should also consider protecting the tasks where human contact is most valued, such as socially and empathically relevant exchanges <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Li & Bitterly, 2024)</ref>, rather than automating them by default.

text.text: These shifts sit within a broader change to the employment relationship itself; generative AI and autonomous agents are rewriting the social contract of employment, changing how expertise is recognized, how authority is distributed, and how relationships form at work (Valentine, 2025). Makarius et al. (2020) offer a practical framework for this transition, describing AI integration as a process of building sociotechnical capital along cognitive, relational, and structural dimensions.

text.text: The organizations best positioned to adopt AI successfully may be those that invest as deliberately in the relational conditions surrounding its use, including usage norms, leader support, and team climate, as they do in the technology itself.
Several methodological patterns qualify how confidently these findings can be generalized.
Much of this literature relies on multi-wave employee surveys, often collected in China, South Korea, or Taiwan, paired with scenario-based experiments and analyzed with moderated mediation models.

Selfreport measures are often used, and AI usage is operationalized inconsistently across studies, sometimes as frequency, sometimes as collaboration intensity, and sometimes as organizational investment.

The stronger causal evidence, drawn from field experiments (Tang et al., 2023; Tey et al., 2024), incentivized behavioral games (Leib et al., 2023; Harrell & Traeger, 2025a , 2025b), and large-scale archival analysis (Safadi et al., 2024), is concentrated in a smaller subset of studies and would benefit from replication across more industries and cultural contexts.

text.text: Several studies rely on student rather than employee samples (Zhang et al., 2026a), and robots, chatbots, and generative AI are often treated as interchangeable despite likely differences in the relational signals each conveys.

text.text: Longitudinal work is needed to understand whether these effects persist, intensify, or habituate as AI use becomes normalized, since most current designs capture a single point in time or a short panel.

The literature is heavily skewed toward documenting the costs of AI; the conditions under which AI can be designed to support rather than substitute for human connection remain underexplored, despite promising exceptions such as Shirado and Christakis (2017).
text.formatted: The literature is heavily skewed toward documenting the costs of AI; the conditions under which AI can be designed to support rather than substitute for human connection remain underexplored, despite promising exceptions such as <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Shirado and Christakis (2017)</ref>.

text.text: Intervention research testing specific organizational policies is similarly scarce, as is research at the team and network level rather than the dyad.

Since disclosure does not appear to restore trust (Schilke & Reimann, 2025), future work should test what does: which usage norms avoid the degradation of trust without concealing AI use, how credit and blame should be allocated for AI-assisted work, and what relational-skill training should accompany AI literacy training, given the risk that relational skills may erode without use (Keeler & Murphy, 2026).

text.text: Taken as a whole, this literature suggests that AI's costs to workplace relationships run mostly through indirect pathways, through how coworkers attribute motive, how they calibrate trust and moral judgment, and how they choose to reciprocate, rather than through any inherent property of the technology itself.
